extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Tatler; literate coffee-house public and contemporary readers interested in theatre, poetry, and manners (early 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A short periodical/essayistic treatment of contemporary theatre, poetry, and social manners offering prescriptive remarks on poetic diction, dramatic practice, conversational behaviour, and the social effects of the stage. Written for a general literate readership in the early 1700s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate rhyme and diction in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic language and rhyme must be natural and not forced; awkward or ill-fitting rhymes spoil verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original warning: 'Avail and toil, defect and tract, will never do for rhymes.' The commentator critiques his kinsman's heroic lines and advises avoiding unnatural word choices and forced rhymes that betray weakness in versification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in depicting death (avoid theatrical ostentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals of dying should be natural, not theatrical or staged according to rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘None but a tragedian can die by rule… In real life, this is a chimera.’ Praises 'natural greatness of soul' — genuine, unostentatious behaviour is superior to artificial sentiments or contrived speeches on a deathbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should produce vivid, reflective imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry supplies lively images that give pleasure and fix reflections in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised example: Philips' winter-piece gives 'such images as these give us a new pleasure… and fix upon our minds traces of reflection.' Guidance: employ striking description that prompts ongoing reflection and delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and good breeding in conversation; avoid 'biters'
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of behaviour is the perfection of good breeding and good sense; avoid the contemporary 'biter' (a sneerer who entraps and exposes others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the essay: 'simplicity of behaviour, which is the perfection of good breeding and good sense, is utterly lost…' and the definition of a 'Biter' (one who tells a plausible lie to expose the other). Advice: favour plain, sincere wit over contemptuous sneering that humiliates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre must prioritize wit, humour, and good sense over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should emphasize action, character, wit, and good sense rather than rely on exotic spectacles, dances, and acrobatic amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of contemporary management: managers have introduced 'ladder-dancers, rope-dancers, jugglers, and mountebanks' in place of Shakespearean heroes. 'Wit and spirit, humour and good sense, can never be revived' unless theatre is governed by those who appreciate such talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre management should be led by knowledgeable judges of talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Revival of true wit and dramatic quality requires governance by people qualified to judge theatrical talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that 'those who are judges of such talents' must govern the stage; mere entrepreneurs/money-men (Divito) or uninformed managers mortgage the muse and degrade performance. Implies selection, oversight, and leadership are criteria for theatrical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre-makers bear social responsibility — stage influences manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The content and conduct of the theatre materially affect public manners and morals and so must be treated with responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: 'the theatre has much the same effect on the manners of the age, as the bank on the credit of the nation.' Guidance: practitioners should be mindful that theatrical fashions shape societal taste and behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use satire and allegory effectively to critique power
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic devices (e.g., dances, allegories) may be used as satire to expose political and social dynamics (such as absolute vs free government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the play: a dance representing 'absolute power' (a tall man with a hat and feather who gives his minister a huge kick, passing down) versus a dance representing 'a free state' (players moving round and kicking as friends and equals). Guidance: allegorical staging can illuminate political critique when done cleverly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false or inauthentic presentation of performers (authentic casting/voices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers and musical elements should be genuine; managers should not pass off inauthentic or artificially produced talents on the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical admonition: the theatre has been 'put into the hands of a surgeon, who cuts any foreign fellow into an eunuch, and passes him upon us for a singer of Italy.' Guidance: do not present harmful or fraudulent practices to simulate talent — prioritize authentic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing non-essential entertainments without proper authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel entertainments (ladders, antic postures, etc.) that do not serve to better the performance should be regulated and not introduced without official leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote cites Lord Chamberlain's warrant ordering that 'no new representations… which are not necessary to the better performance of comedy or opera, such as ladder-dancing, antic postures, &c., without his leave.' Practical guidance: restrain superfluous spectacle; secure proper permission for innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic treatment of mortality should encourage living well rather than empty doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflections on death in poetry should point to the importance of living well; moralizing that lacks practical virtue is empty labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary: 'All which glory and shame must end in what we so much repine at, death. But doctrines on this occasion, any other than that of living well, are the most insignificant and most empty of all the labours of men.' Guidance: moral seriousness and utility should guide poetic reflections on mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire is an appropriate device to correct social follies (e.g., enthusiasm, modern prophets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical drama can effectively expose and correct social errors and fanaticisms by turning humour and imitated traits to ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: D'Urfey's 'Modern Prophets' is praised as 'a most unanswerable satire against the late spirit of enthusiasm,' and Punch turning prophet ended the fanatics. Guidance: well-executed satire on stage can shape public opinion and curb follies.
